The Tigris River. One of the two great rivers of ancient Mesopotamia, flowing approximately nineteen hundred kilometers from its source in southeastern Turkey through Iraq to the Persian Gulf. Along with the Euphrates, it cradled one of humanity's earliest civilizations and continues to be critical to Iraq's agriculture and water supply, though shared between Turkey, Syria, Iraq, and Iran.

The Tigris originates in the Taurus Mountains of southeastern Turkey and flows southeast through Iraq, ultimately merging with the Euphrates near the Persian Gulf. Ancient Assyria flourished on the Tigris's banks. Cities like Ashur, Nineveh, and Babylon rose to dominance through control of the river. The Tigris-Euphrates system supported the rise of writing, law codes, agriculture, and urban civilization in ancient Mesopotamia.

The rivers merge near Basra in southern Iraq, and their combined delta extends into the Persian Gulf where it is ecologically significant. But water diversion for dams in Turkey and Syria has reduced the Tigris's flow to Iraq by up to eighty percent in some seasons. The river is shared by four nations, and tensions over dam construction and water allocation remain a source of political friction. Archaeological sites like Nineveh and Assur line the riverbanks, preserving layers of human civilization.
